# How to use this notebook

This brings together everything from the class notes and the class RPubs page,
plus the pieces that were only mentioned in passing (chi-square, ANOVA, MANOVA,
regression assumptions, dplyr, ggplot2).

Work through it with the green ▶ on each chunk, one chunk at a time, in order.
Change the numbers and re-run. Breaking something and fixing it is the fastest
way to remember it.

Each part ends with a **Practice** block. The answers are in the last section,
so try first and check after.

```{r packages}
pkgs <- c("dplyr", "ggplot2")
new_pkgs <- pkgs[!pkgs %in% rownames(installed.packages())]
if (length(new_pkgs) > 0) install.packages(new_pkgs, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")

library(ggplot2)
```

# Part 1 — Data structures

Everything in R is built from a handful of structures. Knowing which one you are
holding explains most error messages you will ever get.

## Vectors

A vector is a row of values **of one single type**. `c()` ("combine") builds one.

```{r vectors}
# numeric
age <- c(20, 35, 32, 29)
age
mean(age)
summary(age)

# character
gender <- c("M", "F", "F", "M")
gender

# logical
flags <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
flags
# T and F are short forms of the same thing
c(T, F)

# integer: the colon makes a sequence
x <- 9:29
x

# complex (rare in data work, but it is a type)
c(1 + 0i, 2 + 4i)
```

`class()` tells you which type you ended up with:

```{r vector-class}
class(age)
class(gender)
class(flags)
class(9:29)
```

## The bracket trick

Assigning with `<-` stores a value **silently**. Wrapping the whole line in
round brackets stores *and* prints it. Handy while exploring, so you do not have
to type the name again on the next line.

```{r bracket-trick}
y <- c(1, 2, 3)        # silent, nothing appears
(y <- c(1, 2, 3))      # same assignment, but the result is printed
```

## Coercion

A vector cannot mix types, so if you force different types together R quietly
converts them all to the most flexible one. This is **coercion**, and it is a
very common source of bugs.

```{r coercion}
# TRUE becomes 1 and FALSE becomes 0, so logicals can be summed
sum(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE))

# one piece of text turns the entire vector into text
mixed <- c(1, 2, "three")
class(mixed)
mixed

# which means arithmetic now fails
# mean(mixed)   # uncomment to see the error

# as.numeric() converts back where possible; anything else becomes NA
as.numeric(c("10", "20", "abc"))
```

## Matrices

A matrix is a vector folded into rows and columns. Still one single type.

```{r matrix}
(x <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3))
(y <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2))

dim(x)        # rows, columns

x %*% y       # %*% is real matrix multiplication
x * 2         # a single * works element by element
t(x)          # transpose
```

## Lists

A list is the flexible one: each slot can hold anything, even another list.

```{r list}
(mylist <- list(1, "a", TRUE, 1 + 4i))

# naming the slots makes a list much easier to use
person <- list(name = "Aline", age = 23, scores = c(78, 85, 91))
person$name
person$scores
person$scores[2]
```

## Factors

A factor is a **categorical** variable. It looks like text but R stores it as
numbers with labels, and remembers the full set of possible values (the levels).
Statistical functions treat factors as groups, which is exactly what you want
for a variable like gender or species.

```{r factor}
(status <- factor(c("yes", "yes", "no", "yes", "no")))
levels(status)
table(status)

# as.integer() shows the numbers hiding underneath
as.integer(status)
```

## Missing values

`NA` means "not available". It is not zero and it is not the text `"NA"`.

```{r missing}
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 10, 3)
is.na(x)

# most calculations refuse to guess, so they return NA
mean(x)
# na.rm = TRUE says "ignore the missing ones"
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)

# keep only the good values: ! flips TRUE and FALSE
bad <- is.na(x)
x[!bad]

# complete.cases() works across several vectors at once:
# TRUE only where BOTH have a value
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4, NA, 5)
y <- c("a", "b", NA, "d", NA, "f")
(good <- complete.cases(x, y))
```

Watch out for the trap in the class notes:

```{r missing-trap}
x <- c(1, 2, 4, "NA", 5)   # "NA" in quotes is just text
is.na(x)                   # all FALSE: R sees no missing value here
class(x)                   # and the whole vector became character
```

## Data frames

A data frame is the one you will use most: a table where each column is a vector
and **different columns may hold different types**. It is R's spreadsheet.

```{r dataframe}
studentID  <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
gender     <- c("M", "F", "M", "M", "F")
math_score <- c(12, 17, 10, 9, NA)
it_score   <- c(13, 18, 11, 10, 19)

scoredata <- data.frame(studentID, gender, math_score, it_score)
scoredata

str(scoredata)    # structure: the single most useful check
nrow(scoredata)
ncol(scoredata)
dim(scoredata)
names(scoredata)
```

`View(scoredata)` opens it as a spreadsheet, and `edit()` lets you type data by
hand. Both only work in RStudio, never while knitting, so they are switched off
here.

```{r interactive, eval=FALSE}
View(scoredata)

# typing a small dataset straight into a window
data_class2 <- data.frame(height = numeric(0),
                          weight = numeric(0),
                          bmi    = numeric(0))
data_class2 <- edit(data_class2)
```

# Part 2 — The class dataset

The class used a file of heights and weights. We do not have that exact file, so
this chunk creates a very similar one and saves it. `set.seed()` fixes the random
numbers so you get the same data every time you run it.

```{r make-class-data}
set.seed(2026)

n <- 40
HEIGHT <- round(rnorm(n, mean = 170, sd = 9), 0)
# weight is built from height plus noise, so the two are genuinely related
WEIGHT <- round(0.55 * HEIGHT - 25 + rnorm(n, 0, 4), 0)

data_class <- data.frame(HEIGHT, WEIGHT)

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.table(data_class, "data/class_data.txt", row.names = FALSE)

head(data_class)
```

Now read it back, the way the class did with their own file:

```{r read-class-data}
data_class <- read.table("data/class_data.txt", header = TRUE)
head(data_class)
```

`header = TRUE` matters: without it `read.table()` treats the names row as data
and every column arrives as text.

# Part 3 — Looking at the data

The first five minutes with any dataset are always the same four commands.

```{r first-look}
head(data_class)        # first 6 rows
tail(data_class)        # last 6 rows
str(data_class)         # how many rows, which columns, which types
summary(data_class)     # min, Q1, median, mean, Q3, max for every column
```

`summary()` on a single column gives the five-number summary plus the mean:

```{r summary-one}
summary(data_class$WEIGHT)
length(data_class$WEIGHT)
variable.names(data_class)
```

## Reaching inside a data frame

```{r subsetting-basics}
# $ pulls out one column as a vector
data_class$WEIGHT[1:5]

# [rows, columns] — leave a side empty to mean "all of it"
data_class[10:20, ]      # rows 10 to 20, every column
data_class[, 1]          # column 1, every row
data_class[5, 2]         # one single cell
data_class[1:3, "HEIGHT"]

# a minus sign DROPS instead of keeping
head(data_class[, -1])   # everything except column 1
```

## `$` versus `[ ]` versus `[[ ]]`

This confuses everybody at first. The rule is about **what comes back**.

```{r brackets}
# single [ ] keeps the data frame shape
class(data_class["HEIGHT"])
# $ and [[ ]] dig out the bare vector inside
class(data_class$HEIGHT)
class(data_class[["HEIGHT"]])
```

Use `$` when you want the values, and `[ ]` when you want a smaller table.
`[[ ]]` does the same job as `$` but accepts a variable holding the name, which
is what makes it useful inside loops and functions:

```{r brackets-2}
wanted <- "WEIGHT"
head(data_class[[wanted]])     # works
head(data_class$wanted)        # NULL: R looked for a column literally called "wanted"
```

## Built-in datasets

R ships with datasets for practising. `data()` lists them in a new tab in
RStudio, which is why nothing appears in the console.

```{r builtin-datasets}
# the names only, so it prints here too
head(data()$results[, c("Package", "Item")], 10)
```

Load one and read its help page. `?airquality` explains every column — always
worth doing before you analyse anything.

```{r load-airquality}
data("airquality")
str(airquality)
variable.names(airquality)
```

```{r help-page, eval=FALSE}
?airquality
?apply
```

Copying a dataset to your own name keeps the original safe while you experiment:

```{r rename-dataset}
air <- airquality
head(air, 3)
```

# Part 4 — Summary statistics

## Mean, SD and the quartiles

```{r stats-basic}
mean(data_class$HEIGHT)
sd(data_class$HEIGHT)
median(data_class$HEIGHT)
min(data_class$HEIGHT)
max(data_class$HEIGHT)
range(data_class$HEIGHT)
var(data_class$HEIGHT)

# quantile() is where Q1 and Q3 in summary() come from
quantile(data_class$HEIGHT)
quantile(data_class$HEIGHT, 0.25)   # first quartile on its own
IQR(data_class$HEIGHT)              # Q3 - Q1
```

## Reporting two numbers together

`c()` glues results into one labelled vector. Naming the parts makes the output
readable, which matters when you paste it into a report.

```{r stats-c}
# without names
c(mean(data_class$HEIGHT), sd(data_class$HEIGHT))

# with names — much clearer
c(Mean = mean(data_class$HEIGHT), SD = sd(data_class$HEIGHT))
c(Mean = mean(data_class$WEIGHT), SD = sd(data_class$WEIGHT))
```

## `apply()` and friends

`apply()` runs the same function down every column or across every row.
The middle number is the direction: **1 = rows, 2 = columns**.

```{r apply}
# the mean of each row (here: the average of a person's height and weight,
# which is not meaningful, but it shows the mechanics)
head(apply(data_class, 1, mean))

# the standard deviation of each column — this one is useful
apply(data_class, 2, sd)
apply(data_class, 2, mean)
apply(data_class, 2, summary)
```

Remember the direction with: **1 before 2, rows before columns**.

For plain sums and means there are faster ready-made versions:

```{r rowcolsums}
colSums(data_class)
colMeans(data_class)
head(rowSums(data_class))

# na.rm = TRUE is needed whenever the data has gaps
colMeans(airquality)                 # NA wherever a column has missing values
colMeans(airquality, na.rm = TRUE)   # the answer you actually wanted
```

# Part 5 — Bivariate analysis

Looking at two variables together. Which tool you reach for depends entirely on
the **types** of the two variables, so it is worth memorising this table:

| Variable 1 | Variable 2 | Look at it with | Test it with |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quantitative | Quantitative | scatter plot, `cor()` | `cor.test()`, `lm()` |
| Categorical | Quantitative | boxplot, `by()` | t-test (2 groups), ANOVA (3+) |
| Categorical | Categorical | `table()`, bar chart | chi-square test |

## 5.1 Quantitative vs quantitative

```{r scatter}
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class,
     main = "Weight against height", xlab = "Height (cm)", ylab = "Weight (kg)")

# the same plot written the other way round: plot(x, y)
plot(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT, main = "Same plot, different syntax")

# and by column position
plot(data_class[, 1], data_class[, 2], main = "Graph")
```

Correlation puts a number on the strength of that relationship, between −1 and
+1:

```{r correlation}
cor(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)
```

`cor()` gives the number. `cor.test()` also tells you whether it is strong
enough to take seriously, with a p-value and a confidence interval:

```{r cor-test}
cor.test(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)
```

A p-value below 0.05 means a correlation this far from zero would be unlikely if
the two variables were truly unrelated.

## 5.2 Categorical vs quantitative

The question here is always the same: **does the average change from group to
group?**

```{r iris-groups}
data("iris")
head(iris)

# overall mean, ignoring the groups
mean(iris$Petal.Length)

# one group at a time, by filtering inside the square brackets
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "setosa"])
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "versicolor"])
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "virginica"])
```

Note the double `==`. One `=` assigns, two `==` compares. Writing `=` by mistake
is one of the most common beginner errors.

`by()` does all three at once, which is the shortcut from class:

```{r by}
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, mean)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, sd)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, summary)
```

`tapply()` does the same and returns a tidy named vector:

```{r tapply}
tapply(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, mean)
aggregate(Petal.Length ~ Species, data = iris, FUN = mean)
```

### Visualising it: the boxplot

A boxplot is the standard picture for categorical against quantitative. The box
runs from Q1 to Q3, the thick line is the median, the whiskers reach the rest of
the data and the dots are outliers.

```{r boxplot}
boxplot(iris$Sepal.Length ~ iris$Species, data = iris,
        main = "Comparison of categorical vs quantitative",
        xlab = "Species", ylab = "Sepal length (cm)",
        col = c("lightblue", "lightgreen", "pink"))
```

The `~` means "by" or "explained by": `Sepal.Length ~ Species` reads as
"sepal length broken down by species".

### Testing it: ANOVA

The boxplot suggests the groups differ. ANOVA (analysis of variance) checks
whether that difference is bigger than random variation would explain.

The hypotheses, written out:

- **H₀** (null): all the group means are equal, μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃
- **H₁** (alternative): at least one mean is different

```{r anova}
fit_aov <- aov(Sepal.Length ~ Species, data = iris)
summary(fit_aov)
```

Read the `Pr(>F)` column. It is far below 0.05, so we reject H₀: the species
really do differ in sepal length.

ANOVA only says "at least one differs". `TukeyHSD()` says **which** ones:

```{r tukey}
TukeyHSD(fit_aov)
```

With only two groups you would use a t-test instead:

```{r ttest}
two_species <- iris[iris$Species != "virginica", ]
t.test(Sepal.Length ~ Species, data = two_species)
```

### MANOVA

ANOVA handles one response variable. MANOVA handles several at once, which is
useful when the outcomes are related, as petal and sepal measurements are.

```{r manova}
fit_man <- manova(cbind(Sepal.Length, Petal.Length) ~ Species, data = iris)
summary(fit_man)

# and the individual ANOVAs behind it
summary.aov(fit_man)
```

## 5.3 Categorical vs categorical

Here the tool is a **cross-tabulation**: a table of counts.

```{r table-basic}
table(iris$Species)

# two variables at once gives a contingency table
ucba <- data.frame(UCBAdmissions)
head(ucba)
```

`UCBAdmissions` is already summarised: each row is a count (`Freq`), not a
person. `xtabs()` builds a table from counts like these.

```{r xtabs}
(cross <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba))
```

Raw counts are hard to compare when the groups are different sizes, so convert
to proportions. The second argument is the direction again: **1 = by row**.

```{r proptable}
prop.table(cross, 1)    # each ROW adds to 1: admission rate within each gender
prop.table(cross, 2)    # each COLUMN adds to 1
prop.table(cross)       # everything adds to 1
```

**Is there gender bias in UCB graduate admission?** On these numbers about 44%
of men were admitted against about 30% of women. Hold that thought for Part 6.

### Testing it: chi-square

The chi-square test of independence asks whether two categorical variables are
related.

- **H₀**: the two variables are independent (gender and admission are unrelated)
- **H₁**: they are not independent

```{r chisq}
chisq.test(cross)
```

A p-value under 0.05 rejects independence. You can look at what the table would
have been under H₀:

```{r chisq-expected}
test <- chisq.test(cross)
test$expected    # counts expected if gender and admission were unrelated
test$observed    # what actually happened
round(test$residuals, 2)   # where the biggest departures are
```

Chi-square needs reasonably large expected counts (a common rule is at least 5
in each cell). For small tables, use Fisher's exact test instead:

```{r fisher}
fisher.test(cross)
```

### Visualising it: bar charts

```{r barcharts}
# side by side: best for comparing groups directly
barplot(cross, beside = TRUE, legend = TRUE,
        main = "Side-by-side bar chart", col = c("steelblue", "tomato"))

# stacked: best for showing composition of a total
barplot(cross, beside = FALSE, legend = TRUE,
        main = "Stacked bar chart", col = c("steelblue", "tomato"))
```

The two bar charts from the class notes, built from a typed table:

```{r barplot-class}
dat <- read.table(text = "ProdA ProdB ProdC ProdD
1 110 50 60 70
2 120 50 80 65", header = TRUE)
barplot(as.matrix(dat), beside = TRUE, col = c("red", "green"),
        main = "Products, two periods")

dat2 <- read.table(text = "A   B   C   D   E   F    G
1 10 80 30 90 70 60  90
2 20 50 70 50 40 10  40
3 60 80 80 60 60 30 160
4 20 40 70 80 20 10  70", header = TRUE)
barplot(as.matrix(dat2), main = "Stacked by default")
```

Note `read.table(text = "...")` — a neat way to type a small table directly
into your code instead of creating a file.

# Part 6 — Simpson's paradox

This is the most important idea in the whole class, because it is how a correct
calculation can still give the wrong answer.

Overall, men were admitted at a much higher rate than women:

```{r simpson-overall}
prop.table(cross, 1)
```

Now look at the same data **one department at a time**:

```{r simpson-by-dept}
for (d in levels(ucba$Dept)) {
  cat("\n--- Department", d, "---\n")
  tab <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba[ucba$Dept == d, ])
  print(round(prop.table(tab, 1), 3))
}
```

In most individual departments women were admitted at the **same or a higher**
rate than men. The overall figure reverses once you split the data up. That
reversal is **Simpson's paradox**.

The explanation is a hidden third variable: women applied in larger numbers to
departments that reject most applicants, while men applied to easier ones.

```{r simpson-explanation}
# how hard each department is overall
round(prop.table(xtabs(Freq ~ Dept + Admit, data = ucba), 1), 3)

# where each gender applied
xtabs(Freq ~ Dept + Gender, data = ucba)
```

The lesson: **always ask what you have not split by.** An aggregate number can
hide, or even invert, what is happening underneath.

## Frequentist and Bayesian thinking

Two different ways of answering "what does this data tell me?", mentioned in
class:

- **Frequentist**: treats the truth as fixed and the data as random. It asks
  "if H₀ were true, how surprising is data like mine?" That is what a p-value
  measures. Everything in this notebook so far is frequentist.
- **Bayesian**: starts from a prior belief, collects data, and updates that
  belief into a posterior. It answers the question people usually *think* a
  p-value answers: "how likely is my hypothesis, given this data?"

Neither is "correct". Frequentist methods dominate teaching and journals;
Bayesian methods suit problems with real prior knowledge or little data.

# Part 7 — Linear models

Regression draws the best straight line through a scatter plot, so you can
describe and predict.

```{r lm-plot}
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class, main = "With fitted line")
abline(lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class), col = "red", lwd = 2)

# lowess adds a flexible smooth curve: if it bends far from the straight
# line, a straight line was the wrong choice
lines(lowess(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("linear", "lowess"),
       col = c("red", "blue"), lty = 1)
```

## Fitting and reading the model

```{r lm-fit}
model <- lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
model              # just the coefficients
summary(model)     # the full report
```

How to read `summary()`:

- **Estimate** for `HEIGHT` is the slope: how many kg the weight goes up for
  each extra cm of height.
- **(Intercept)** is the predicted weight at height 0 — usually meaningless on
  its own, it just positions the line.
- **Pr(>|t|)** is the p-value for the slope. Below 0.05 means the relationship
  is statistically significant.
- **R-squared** is the share of the variation in weight that height explains,
  so a value of 0.60 would mean 60%. Check what this model actually gives
  below, and remember that a high R-squared still does not prove that height
  *causes* weight.

Pulling out the pieces separately:

```{r lm-parts}
coef(model)
confint(model)                 # 95% confidence interval for the slope
head(fitted(model))            # the predicted values
head(residuals(model))         # observed minus predicted
summary(model)$r.squared
```

Predicting for new people:

```{r lm-predict}
new_people <- data.frame(HEIGHT = c(160, 175, 190))
predict(model, newdata = new_people)
predict(model, newdata = new_people, interval = "confidence")
```

## Checking the assumptions

A model only means something if its assumptions hold. `plot(model)` draws four
diagnostic pictures — this is the step from your notes.

```{r lm-diagnostics, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))    # 2 x 2 grid of plots
plot(model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))    # back to one plot at a time
```

What to look for in each:

| Plot | Assumption | Good sign |
|---|---|---|
| Residuals vs Fitted | linearity | points scattered randomly, red line flat |
| Q-Q Residuals | residuals are normal | points follow the diagonal |
| Scale-Location | equal variance | even band, no funnel shape |
| Residuals vs Leverage | no single point dominates | nothing past the dashed Cook's line |

The four assumptions in words: the relationship is **linear**, the errors are
**independent**, their spread is **constant** (homoscedasticity), and they are
roughly **normally distributed**.

You can also test them formally:

```{r lm-tests}
# are the residuals normal? p > 0.05 means no evidence against normality
shapiro.test(residuals(model))

# a histogram of the residuals should look roughly bell-shaped
hist(residuals(model), col = "lightblue", main = "Residuals", xlab = "Residual")
```

## Multiple regression

More than one explanatory variable: just add them with `+`.

```{r multiple-lm}
air_model <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp + Wind + Solar.R, data = airquality)
summary(air_model)
```

Each slope is now the effect of that variable **holding the others fixed**.

```{r histograms}
hist(data_class$HEIGHT, main = "Height", xlab = "cm")
hist(data_class$WEIGHT, col = "blue", main = "Weight", xlab = "kg")
```

# Part 8 — Data management

Real data always needs work before it can be analysed.

## Creating new variables

```{r new-variable}
# attach() lets you type HEIGHT instead of data_class$HEIGHT
attach(data_class)

BMI <- WEIGHT / (HEIGHT / 100)^2
(BMI <- round(WEIGHT / (HEIGHT / 100)^2, digits = 2))

detach(data_class)   # always detach when finished
```

`attach()` is convenient but risky: if a column shares a name with something
already in your workspace, R may silently use the wrong one. Safer habits are
`data_class$HEIGHT`, or `with()`:

```{r with}
BMI <- with(data_class, round(WEIGHT / (HEIGHT / 100)^2, 2))
head(BMI)
```

## `cbind()` and `rbind()`

`cbind` glues **c**olumns side by side, `rbind` stacks **r**ows underneath.

```{r cbind-rbind}
new_data_class <- cbind(data_class, BMI)
head(new_data_class, 5)
tail(new_data_class, 3)

# adding rows: the new data must have the same columns
extra <- data.frame(HEIGHT = c(168, 181), WEIGHT = c(62, 79), BMI = c(21.97, 24.11))
rbind(head(new_data_class, 2), extra)
```

The simplest way to add one column is just to name it:

```{r add-column}
new_data_class$category <- ifelse(new_data_class$BMI < 18.5, "Underweight",
                           ifelse(new_data_class$BMI < 25, "Normal",
                           ifelse(new_data_class$BMI < 30, "Overweight", "Obese")))
head(new_data_class)
table(new_data_class$category)
```

`ifelse(test, value_if_true, value_if_false)` works down the whole column at
once, and nesting it gives you several categories.

## Stem-and-leaf

An old-fashioned text histogram that keeps the actual digits. `scale` makes it
taller or shorter.

```{r stem}
summary(BMI)
stem(BMI, scale = 2)
```

## Dates

```{r dates}
today <- Sys.Date()
today
format(today, format = "%B %d %Y")
format(today, format = "%A")

dob <- as.Date("1982-02-10")
difftime(today, dob, units = "days")

startdate <- as.Date("2004-02-13")
enddate   <- as.Date("2011-01-22")
(days <- enddate - startdate)

as.numeric(days) / 365.25   # roughly how many years
```

Common format codes: `%Y` four-digit year, `%m` month number, `%d` day,
`%B` month name, `%A` weekday name.

## Handling missing values

The leadership example from class:

```{r leadership}
manager <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
country <- c("US", "US", "UK", "UK", "UK")
gender  <- c("M", "F", "F", "M", "F")
age     <- c(32, 45, 25, 39, 99)
q1 <- c(5, 3, 3, 3, 2)
q2 <- c(4, 5, 5, 3, 2)
q3 <- c(5, 2, 5, 4, 1)
q4 <- c(5, 5, 5, NA, 2)
q5 <- c(5, 5, 2, NA, 1)

leadership <- data.frame(manager, country, gender, age,
                         q1, q2, q3, q4, q5, stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
str(leadership)
names(leadership)
```

The age of 99 is not a real age — it is a code meaning "missing". Fix it first,
otherwise every average you calculate is wrong:

```{r recode-missing}
leadership$age[leadership$age == 99] <- NA
leadership$age

is.na(leadership[, 5:9])
```

Then build an age category from the cleaned column:

```{r agecat}
leadership$agecat[leadership$age > 75] <- "Elder"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age >= 35 & leadership$age <= 75] <- "Middle Aged"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age < 35] <- "Young"
leadership[, c("manager", "age", "agecat")]
```

`&` means AND, `|` means OR.

```{r na-omit}
# na.omit() drops every row with any NA anywhere.
# Simple, but it can throw away a lot of data — check how much first.
newdata <- na.omit(leadership)
nrow(leadership)
nrow(newdata)
newdata
```

## Sorting

```{r sorting}
order(leadership$age)                 # the row numbers in sorted order
leadership[order(leadership$age), ]   # the data frame sorted by age

# decreasing, and sorting by two keys
head(leadership[order(-leadership$age), c("manager", "age")])
head(leadership[order(leadership$gender, leadership$age), c("gender", "age")])
```

`order()` returns positions, not values. That is why it goes **inside** the
square brackets.

## Subsetting

```{r subset-vars}
# by position
newdata3 <- leadership[, c(5:9)]
head(newdata3, 3)

# by name — easier to read and it survives column reordering
myvars <- c("q1", "q2", "q3", "q4", "q5")
head(leadership[myvars], 3)

# dropping with minus
head(leadership[, c(-1, -2)], 3)
head(leadership[, -(1:5)], 3)

# rows
leadership[c(2, 4, 5), ]     # keep these rows
leadership[c(-1, -3), ]      # drop these rows
```

`subset()` reads more like a sentence and is the easiest to get right:

```{r subset-fn}
subset(leadership, age >= 35 | age < 24, select = c(q1, q2, q3, q4, q5))
subset(leadership, gender == "M" & age > 30)
```

## Merging datasets

Joining two tables on a shared key, the same idea as a SQL `JOIN`.

```{r merge}
scores <- data.frame(manager = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
                     bonus   = c(500, 700, 450, 800, 600))

merged <- merge(leadership, scores, by = "manager")
merged[, c("manager", "country", "age", "bonus")]
```

`all = TRUE` keeps unmatched rows from both sides (a full outer join);
`all.x = TRUE` keeps everything from the left table (a left join).

# Part 9 — dplyr

dplyr does the same jobs as Part 8 but with five verbs that read like English.
The pipe `%>%` passes the result on the left into the function on the right, so
you can chain steps in the order you think of them.

| Verb | Job |
|---|---|
| `filter()` | keep certain **rows** |
| `select()` | keep certain **columns** |
| `mutate()` | add or change a column |
| `arrange()` | sort |
| `summarise()` | collapse to a single row |
| `group_by()` | do all of the above per group |

```{r dplyr-basics}
iris %>% filter(Species == "setosa") %>% head(3)

iris %>% select(Species, Petal.Length) %>% head(3)

iris %>%
  mutate(Petal.Area = Petal.Length * Petal.Width) %>%
  select(Species, Petal.Length, Petal.Width, Petal.Area) %>%
  head(3)

iris %>% arrange(desc(Petal.Length)) %>% head(3)
```

The real power is `group_by()` plus `summarise()`, which replaces `by()` and
gives a tidy data frame back:

```{r dplyr-group}
iris %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarise(n       = n(),
            mean_pl = mean(Petal.Length),
            sd_pl   = sd(Petal.Length),
            max_pl  = max(Petal.Length))
```

Chaining several steps:

```{r dplyr-chain}
airquality %>%
  filter(!is.na(Ozone)) %>%
  mutate(hot = Temp > 80) %>%
  group_by(Month, hot) %>%
  summarise(mean_ozone = round(mean(Ozone), 1), days = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(Month)
```

The same thing in base R would need several intermediate objects. Compare:

```{r base-vs-dplyr}
# base R
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "setosa"])

# dplyr
iris %>% filter(Species == "setosa") %>% summarise(mean(Petal.Length))
```

Both are correct. Base R is always available; dplyr is easier to read once a
task has more than two steps.

# Part 10 — ggplot2

Base R plots are quick. ggplot2 is for plots you will show other people.

Every ggplot has three parts: the **data**, the **aesthetics** `aes()` which map
columns to things you can see (x, y, colour, size), and one or more **geoms**
which decide what is drawn. You add the layers with `+`.

```{r gg-scatter}
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Petal.Width, colour = Species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Petal width against petal length",
       x = "Petal length (cm)", y = "Petal width (cm)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Adding a fitted line per group is one more layer:

```{r gg-smooth}
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Petal.Width, colour = Species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "With a regression line per species") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Boxplot, the ggplot version of Part 5:

```{r gg-box}
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Sepal length by species") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Bar charts: `position` switches between stacked and side by side.

```{r gg-bars}
ggplot(ucba, aes(x = Gender, y = Freq, fill = Admit)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack") +
  labs(title = "Stacked") + theme_minimal()

ggplot(ucba, aes(x = Gender, y = Freq, fill = Admit)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Side by side") + theme_minimal()

# fill makes every bar the same height, so you compare proportions
ggplot(ucba, aes(x = Gender, y = Freq, fill = Admit)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  labs(title = "Proportions", y = "Share") + theme_minimal()
```

Histogram and density:

```{r gg-hist}
ggplot(data_class, aes(x = HEIGHT)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Height distribution") + theme_minimal()
```

**Facets** split one plot into small multiples — the perfect tool for Simpson's
paradox, because it shows every department at once:

```{r gg-facet, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
ggplot(ucba, aes(x = Gender, y = Freq, fill = Admit)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  facet_wrap(~ Dept, nrow = 1) +
  labs(title = "Admission rate by gender, split by department",
       y = "Share admitted") +
  theme_minimal()
```

That single picture is the whole paradox: the overall gap disappears once each
department is shown separately.

```{r sol-1}
marks <- c(72, 65, 88, 91, 54)
c(Mean = mean(marks), SD = sd(marks))

marks2 <- c(72, 65, 88, 91, "54")
class(marks2)    # character: one quoted value coerced the whole vector

m <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3)
m %*% m

f <- factor(c("low", "high", "low", "medium"))
levels(f)

marks3 <- c(72, 65, NA, 91, 54)
mean(marks3, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r sol-5}

boxplot(Sepal.Width ~ Species, data = iris, col = "lightblue")

summary(aov(Sepal.Width ~ Species, data = iris))
```

## Practice 7

```{r sol-7}
m1 <- lm(Petal.Length ~ Petal.Width, data = iris)
summary(m1)$r.squared

par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(m1); par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

predict(m1, newdata = data.frame(Petal.Width = 1.5))

m2 <- lm(Petal.Length ~ Petal.Width + Sepal.Length, data = iris)
c(one_predictor = summary(m1)$r.squared,
  two_predictors = summary(m2)$r.squared)
```

# Quick reference

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Structure of a dataset | `str(d)` |
| Summary of everything | `summary(d)` |
| First / last rows | `head(d)`, `tail(d)` |
| One column | `d$col`, `d[["col"]]` |
| Rows and columns | `d[rows, cols]`, minus to drop |
| Mean of each column | `apply(d, 2, mean)` or `colMeans(d)` |
| Mean per group | `by(y, g, mean)`, `tapply(y, g, mean)` |
| Frequency table | `table(x)`, `xtabs(Freq ~ a + b, data = d)` |
| Row proportions | `prop.table(tab, 1)` |
| Boxplot by group | `boxplot(y ~ g, data = d)` |
| Correlation | `cor(x, y)`, `cor.test(x, y)` |
| Compare 2 group means | `t.test(y ~ g, data = d)` |
| Compare 3+ group means | `summary(aov(y ~ g, data = d))` |
| Two categorical variables | `chisq.test(tab)` |
| Regression | `summary(lm(y ~ x, data = d))` |
| Check assumptions | `plot(model)` |
| Drop missing rows | `na.omit(d)` |
| Ignore missing in a stat | `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)` |
| Sort | `d[order(d$col), ]` |
| Filter rows | `subset(d, cond)`, `filter(d, cond)` |
| Add a column | `d$new <- ...`, `mutate()` |
| Join two tables | `merge(a, b, by = "key")` |

**The three things that cause most errors:** using `=` where you need `==`,
forgetting `na.rm = TRUE`, and mixing up `1` (rows) and `2` (columns).
